US bond market volatility is at historic levels.

The MOVE index jumped +19% last week, its largest weekly increase since April 2025, following "Liberation Day."

This index is also called the "VIX of bonds" and measures the yield volatility of 2Y, 5Y, 10Y, and 30Y Treasuries.

This marks its 3rd-largest weekly increase since the 2022 bear market.

The move comes as the 10Y Note Yield jumped +17 basis points last week, to 5.17%, its highest level since June 2007.

At the same time, the 30Y Note Yield rose +16 basis points and surpassed 5.50% for the first time since June 2004.

To put this into perspective, in the week ending March 17th, 2023, the MOVE Index surged +29% following the US banking crisis, when 3 regional banks collapsed.

The US Treasury market is experiencing crisis-like volatility.

UPDATED: My current top picks 👇 September 27, 2026

Several of my picks have reported fresh results since the last update. Here’s what has changed, where my conviction stands, and what I’m watching next.

☢️ URANIUM

Producers & Developers

$CCJ – My blue-chip uranium pick. Cameco’s fuel business and its Westinghouse stake give it exposure across the nuclear supply chain. I’m watching the proposed Westinghouse IPO, though its timing remains uncertain.

$KAP – Scale and a strong cost position keep Kazatomprom on my list. Production execution and input costs remain the key things to watch.

$DNN – Phoenix is in full-scale construction. My focus remains on the freeze wall, schedule and costs as Denison turns the project into a producing mine.

$NXE – Rook I construction is underway. Its resource scale is exceptional; financing and delivery now matter most.

$UUUU – The Australian Strategic Materials acquisition adds rare-earth metals and alloy capabilities to Energy Fuels’ uranium exposure. I’m watching how it executes on that broader supply-chain strategy.

$UEC – Burke Hollow is producing, and fiscal 2026 results are due September 29. That update should offer a clearer view of production growth across its U.S. operations.

Explorers

$SYH – Partner Purecore has begun data compilation and target generation at Yurchison. It’s another example of why I like Skyharbour’s mix of flagship exploration and partner-funded projects.

$M.CN – Initial processing tests at Copper Mountain concentrated 83.9% of the uranium into 29.3% of the sample mass. That’s encouraging for the project’s potential processing route, but it’s early test work; scale-up and drill assays still matter.

🥈 SILVER

Producers

$HL – Lucky Friday’s record quarterly production remains a good example of why Hecla is among my preferred silver producers. I’m watching for sustained delivery.

$AG – San Dimas drilling continues to support resource growth. The next test is how effectively First Majestic converts exploration success into mine plans.

$PAAS – Strong Q2 cash generation keeps Pan American on my list. La Colorada Skarn offers longer-term growth, with development decisions and capital needs still to work through.

Explorers & Developers

$HYMC – Following the high-grade Vortex and Brimstone results, Hycroft says metallurgical testing and work on potential processing routes are underway. Those studies are crucial to turning the discoveries into a viable development plan.

$GRSL.V – The September San Marcial results extended mineralization in the SE Area. I’m watching the remaining step-out drilling for evidence of further resource growth.

$JTWO – My wildcard. Sierra Plata has identified seven veins and high-grade surface samples. Trenching, permits and eventual drilling are the next tests; surface samples are not drill intersections.

🟠 COPPER

$CGNT.V – My primary copper exposure. New Mocoa hole MD-073 returned 804 m at 0.56% CuEq, including 103 m at 1.07% CuEq. The company also identified targets beyond the current resource footprint. Continued drilling and the planned Q4 PEA are the catalysts I’m watching.

⚫ GRAPHENE

$HG $HGRAF – Still my largest holding. HydroGraph has filed materials for a shareholder vote on its proposed U.S. redomicile. Texas scale-up and converting customer work into commercial orders remain the milestones that matter most to me.

Disclosure: I have paid partnerships with Myriad Uranium and Skyharbour Resources.

Not financial advice. Please do your own due diligence.

⚡ SUNDAY METALS PULSE — SEPTEMBER 27 ⚡

Four metals. One pulse. No noise.

The week ends with a fascinating divergence:

Industrial metals are screaming SUPPLY.

Precious metals are fighting the FED.

☢️ URANIUM

Another week, another reminder that the nuclear fuel cycle is getting strategic.

Framatome just signed the first commercial contract to supply >5% enriched fuel to an operating US reactor.

X-energy’s new US TRISO fuel facility also reached another construction milestone.

Meanwhile Niger signed an agreement clearing the way toward restarting development of the Madaouela uranium project.

More reactors.
More advanced fuel.
More enrichment capacity needed.

And Kazatomprom recently warned it could easily sell ALL its uranium production into Eastern markets.

The West still needs to secure its pounds.

⚡ COPPER

This is where things are getting VERY interesting.

Copper is hovering around $15,000/t.

Shanghai warehouse stocks have collapsed roughly 70% since June.

LME available stocks are tightening.

The cash market has flipped into backwardation.

Chinese import premiums are near four-year highs.

Yes, Escondida has restarted after its disruption.

But the bigger problem remains:

Copper inventories are piling up in the US while metal becomes increasingly scarce elsewhere.

AI + grids + electrification are colliding with years of insufficient mine investment.

🥈 SILVER

Silver ends the week around $64.

But underneath the price weakness, physical supply keeps throwing up warning signs.

Endeavour Silver’s Guanaceví mine just suffered a ball-mill failure.

Processing capacity:

Normal → ~1,100 t/day
Now → ~600 t/day

Repairs are expected to take around THREE WEEKS.

Meanwhile:

COMEX registered silver remains below 100 Moz.

India is returning to the physical market.

Mine supply remains essentially stagnant.

2026 is still expected to mark the SIXTH consecutive global silver deficit.

Solar thrifting is real.

So is the deficit.

The next thing I want to see?

Investment demand accelerating while inventories keep falling.

That could change this market FAST.

🥇 GOLD

Gold ends the week around $4,275 after another tough week.

The culprit isn’t difficult to find:

US 10Y >5%.
Sticky inflation.
Hawkish Fed.
More rate hikes being priced.

Gold is now down sharply from its 2026 highs.

But here’s the paradox:

The very forces hurting gold today — enormous debt, high borrowing costs, geopolitical instability and persistent inflation — strengthen the longer-term monetary case for owning it.

The battle is simple:

5%+ yields vs monetary insurance.

For now, yields are winning.

🔥 MY SETUP FOR NEXT WEEK

☢️ Uranium — watch contracting and spot activity. The fuel-cycle buildout continues.

⚡ Copper — watch LME/Shanghai inventories. Physical tightness is becoming difficult to ignore.

🥈 Silver — watch COMEX registered stocks and Indian demand. Below 100 Moz keeps my attention.

🥇 Gold — watch US yields. A reversal from 5% could change sentiment quickly.

The common denominator?

SUPPLY.

You can print money.

You can build another data center.

You can announce another reactor.

But you cannot manufacture uranium, copper, silver or gold overnight.

That’s why I keep watching my four metals.

Every. Single. Day.

Astro Teller and I went deep into how moonshots are actually built. His framework starts with a huge problem, not a technology, and combines the audacity to pursue something unlikely with the humility to assume you are probably wrong. 

We talked about why teams should attack the hardest assumption first, what he calls “training the monkey” before building the pedestal, and why the worst outcome is not failure, but allowing a zombie project to consume years of time and capital. 

Astro also shared how AI is reducing the cost of reaching a moonshot and shortening the distance between a crazy idea and the evidence that it might actually work.

Ben Lamm gave us a fascinating look at where biology is heading. We talked about Colossal’s work to bring back entire populations of extinct species, not simply individual animals, and why he believes tens of thousands of mammoths could ultimately be possible. 

We discussed artificial wombs, with Ben predicting that Colossal could birth mammals fully ex utero within 24 months, as well as the growing ability to engineer genotypes, use AI to understand complex biological patterns, and run thousands of simulated experiments before entering the lab. 

His broader point was just as important: if we back up everything else that matters to us, why aren’t we building the infrastructure to back up species?

Hello, everyone,

This month, pain came for us too.

The Joker named his pain Batman. We named ours $MRNA.

We cowards saw storm clouds gathering over the markets and decided to take shelter. We concentrated the portfolio in stocks that should fall less when the market drifts down.

In our field, these are lower-risk stocks because they have already passed the pivotal stage, received approval, or successfully launched their products.

The patent cliff is here, and the big companies need sales now. So these stocks are currently among the main acquisition targets.

And then $MRNA happened to us.

The company’s unexpectedly successful Phase 3 trial in adjuvant melanoma set off not only $MRNA, but the other “dream stocks” too.

Where did the money come from to fund the party? You guessed it: the very stocks we ran to for shelter.

Don’t worry, we’re not here to take your livelihood, lie on the couch and cry while you scribble God-knows-what on paper and mutter “Mmm…” or “Where does that meet you?” as the clock ticks.

We’re here to show you the stocks caught in the slaughter that we believe—based on our own position and from the most subjective point of view possible—will deliver very strong returns once the $MRNA frenzy passes.

Here’s our lineup. The figures show each stock’s discount to the industry, based on 2030 multiples that currently stand at around 11.75x:

$VTRS (47%), $JAZZ (42%), $MDGL (28%), $BBIO (48%), $PRAX (55%), $TGTX (22%), $ABVX (23%), $VERA (59%), $MLYS (51%), $BMRN (45%), $GERN (84%), $IONS (32%), $NBIX (39%), $SNDX (41%), $GRFS (57%), $UTHR (30%), $FMS (49%), $AXSM (41%).

These healthcare stocks, spanning a range of sectors and company sizes, trade at an average discount of 44%. In other words, they would need to rise about 80% to reach industry multiples.

Every year that passes widens the discount, since these companies are growing faster than the industry.

Also, 13 of the 18 have a built-in option in the form of a possible acquisition.

So we’re banging the table: buy yourself a basket of these high-quality, relatively safe and very cheap stocks.

That said, to be fair, this is not a risk-free position in the short term. The trend described above could continue.

It’s a trend driven by retail investors, and those cowboys are a law unto themselves.

Also, by the end of the year, $MRNA is expected to report Phase 2 results in NSCLC and Phase 3 results in RCC.

These are “cold” tumors, with low immune activity, so the odds of success are significantly lower than in melanoma, which is a “hot” tumor.

Bitcoin closed above the May high, which is technically a point for the bulls, and the burden of proof remains with the bears to prove otherwise.

Given that BTC is still <1% away from the May high, it makes it hard to jump to conclusions going into Q4 (as much as I would like to do so). I thought that maybe by now it would either have accepted back below or be much higher, but instead price has barely moved.

Usually after passing the 50W like in 2019/2023, BTC then runs 20-30% within 1-2 weeks. This time, the move has been much more muted, probably because of fears over seasonality and yields heading higher (which is often bearish for long-duration assets like crypto).

Kind of a frustrating time to be honest, because on one hand what makes sense to me would be weakness into Q4, but BTC continues to show strength, making me sincerely question that view. And historically, the weakness often starts before Q4 arrives (which it has not yet so far this time). 

I suppose I should be less deterministic about my views going forward, as this whole move has been extremely humbling.

Mario Bros was just a classic. first game i played on my NES. game with Duck Hunt and the zapper and i got the one with the Power Pad bundled in with World Class Track Meet

Zelda was the first open world exploration game i (and most other people) had ever played. so many secrets on the map that we used to scour strategy guides and discuss it with friends at school. tried bombing every wall in every dungeon

Mega Man 3 didn't invent the formula, but it basically perfected it. the graphics and soundtrack and bosses were just peak

Civilization 1 was probably the first serious strategy game i played on the family's 286 PC. Civ 2 would eventually be a big leap, but 1 was truly epic for the time. really felt like you were managing an empire and piqued my interest in places around the world

Sim City 1 on PC was an epic management simulator. it is probably still better than most city builder shovel ware on mobile app stores. had to really manage a budget to make it work

Streets of Rage 2 was the quintessential beat 'em up brawler. amazing graphics and soundtrack. one of the most fun games you could get together with your friends and just play. closet thing we had to Final Fight at home

Quake is probably the greatest FPS ever created. fully unlocked camera. felt like it came from the future. and running GL Quake with a Monster 3D or similar graphics card was a defining experience. rich online IRC and web communities. amazing mods like CTF and Team Fortress. no other shooter since has done what this one did for me

Civilization 1 was probably the first serious strategy game i played on the family's 286 PC. Civ 2 would eventually be a big leap, but 1 was truly epic for the time. really felt like you were managing an empire and piqued my interest in places around the world

Sim City 1 on PC was an epic management simulator. it is probably still better than most city builder shovel ware on mobile app stores. had to really manage a budget to make it work

Streets of Rage 2 was the quintessential beat 'em up brawler. amazing graphics and soundtrack. one of the most fun games you could get together with your friends and just play. closet thing we had to Final Fight at home

Warcraft II was real-time strategy basically perfected, with an engaging story and characters and art style to boot. but what made this one shine was playing it with friends (modem to modem), and later with IPX over TCP/IP tools like Kali. absolutely crazy experience playing this thing on the internet with other people

Quake is probably the greatest FPS ever created. fully unlocked camera. felt like it came from the future. and running GL Quake with a Monster 3D or similar graphics card was a defining experience. rich online IRC and web communities. amazing mods like CTF and Team Fortress. no other shooter since has done what this one did for me

Diablo defined the ARPG genre. While Diablo 2 perfected it, Diablo 1 was absolutely ground breaking. i remember my first playthrough of this one more than i do many other games (and remember trading an item with someone online i met in a lobby who quickly stole my item and killed me)
